_meta.scope: Canonical terminology: person/creature/place/object/institution/verse_song/idiom names. Canonical spelling follows the project source novel/Alices_Adventures_in_Wonderland_English.md; realistic-adaptation renames go to adapted_name with the source spelling kept in original_name/aliases. All other 8 worldbuilding files must hit this dictionary 100% (dictionary_hit_100pct).
cross_domain_assumptions: Talking-animal and living-playing-card characters (White Rabbit, Mouse, Duchess's household, Cheshire Cat, King/Queen/Knave of Hearts, Gryphon, Mock Turtle, etc.) are categorized here as 'creature' or 'person' strictly per their literal in-source depiction. This dictionary does NOT decide how the realistic adaptation renders them on screen (human actor, costume/role-play, hallucination, metaphor, or removed) -- that reinterpretation decision belongs to bible/cultivation.json SUP-* entries (owned by 02-worldbuilding/magic-cultivation with world), which was still status: skeleton_empty / decision_status: pending_phase2 at the time this file was written.

Alice's physical size changes and the two object transformations (pebbles into cakes, the crying baby into a pig) are recorded in term definitions as the literal source events, with no assumption about whether the realistic register stages them as literal, metaphorical, or psychological -- deferred to SUP-*.

The Wonderland narrative's dream frame (opened implicitly at TERM-0001 'Alice', closed explicitly in ch012) is noted factually in the 'Wonderland' entry (TERM-0054) without asserting whether the adaptation keeps the frame explicit, ambiguous, or removes it -- deferred to world/magic-cultivation and to be confirmed at H1.

adapted_name is left null on every entry in this pass: no realistic-register renames are invented by this agent. Once SUP-* reinterpretation decisions and character/creature realistic designs land in later phases, memory-bible may register renames here via controlled change (WRITE_RULES.md section 5); this dictionary does not preempt that call.

Where two entries risk being confused as the same term (e.g. Dinah vs. the Cheshire Cat, both cats; Alice vs. Mary Ann; Mock Turtle vs. Mock Turtle Soup vs. the song 'Turtle Soup'), the disambiguating clause is folded into each entry's 'definition' text (cross-referencing the other TERM id) rather than a separate field, since the project skeleton's entry_schema for this file has no dedicated disambiguation field.

terms.definition: The protagonist, a girl of about ten (H1 ruling 5.6 A; the confirmed age is recorded on CHAR-alice); the entire Wonderland narrative is framed as her dream while sitting on the riverbank with her sister (see TERM-0054 Wonderland).

first_seen.quote: Alice was beginning to get very tired of sitting by her sister on the bank

terms.definition: Alice's unnamed elder sister, reading on the riverbank at the story's start; she wakes Alice at the end and has a closing reverie of her own (ch012).

first_seen.quote: sitting by her sister on the bank, and of having nothing to do

terms.definition: A girl Alice knows in waking life, ruled out as who she might have been changed into because Ada's hair goes in long ringlets; never appears on stage.

first_seen.quote: I'm sure I'm not Ada

terms.definition: A girl Alice knows in waking life who "knows such a very little"; Alice fears she has been changed into Mabel when her lessons come out wrong. Never appears on stage.

first_seen.quote: I can't be Mabel, for I know all sorts of things

terms.definition: Real historical figure; referenced first as a joke (a French mouse "come over with William the Conqueror") and then quoted from the Mouse's dry history recitation.

first_seen.quote: I daresay it's a French mouse, come over with William the Conqueror

terms.definition: Real historical earls of Mercia and Northumbria, named in the passage the Mouse recites as "the driest thing I know" to dry the party off.

first_seen.quote: Edwin and Morcar, the earls of Mercia and Northumbria

first_seen.quote: the patriotic archbishop of Canterbury, found it advisable

terms.definition: Referenced only as a visual comparison: the Dodo pauses to think in the pose usually shown in pictures of Shakespeare.

terms.definition: The White Rabbit's real housemaid; she never appears on stage. The Rabbit mistakes Alice for her and sends her to fetch gloves and a fan. Distinct from Alice (TERM-0001), who is not actually Mary Ann.

terms.definition: A footman with a fish-like face who delivers the Queen's croquet invitation to the Frog-Footman at the Duchess's door; appears only in this one exchange.

terms.definition: A footman with a round frog-like face who receives the croquet invitation and then sits uselessly by the door, telling Alice there is no use knocking.

first_seen.quote: another footman in livery, with a round face, and large eyes like a frog

terms.definition: Host of the never-ending tea party with the March Hare and Dormouse; stuck at six o'clock ever since he "murdered the time" singing before the Queen. Asks Alice the unanswered riddle "Why is a raven like a writing-desk?" (TERM-0119) and later gives flustered evidence at the trial.

first_seen.quote: last of all this grand procession, came THE KING AND QUEEN OF HEARTS

terms.definition: Playing-card monarch who quietly pardons the Queen's death sentences; acts as judge at the trial of the Knave in ch011-012, reading out the invented Rule Forty-two (TERM-0091).

terms.definition: One of three playing-card gardeners painting the rose-tree; blamed by Five for jogging his elbow while accused of always deserving beheading.

terms.definition: Unnamed royal executioner who argues at the croquet ground that a head cannot be cut off without a body attached, in a three-way dispute with the King and Queen over beheading the Cheshire Cat.

first_seen.quote: there was a dispute going on between the executioner, the King, and the Queen

terms.definition: Character in the nonsense poem "You are old, Father William" (TERM-0106) that the Caterpillar makes Alice recite; an old man who stands on his head and balances eels on his nose.

first_seen.quote: “You are old, Father William,” the young man said

terms.definition: One of the White Rabbit's outdoor helpers, addressed as "Pat" and speaking with an Irish idiom ("yer honour"); species is not specified in the text.

terms.definition: Alice's pet cat back home, mentioned throughout as an object of homesickness and a running threat ("I'll set Dinah at you!"). Never appears in Wonderland; distinct from the Cheshire Cat (TERM-0040), the grinning cat Alice meets in Wonderland.

first_seen.quote: (Dinah was the cat.)

terms.definition: A pink-eyed, waistcoat-and-watch-carrying rabbit whom Alice follows down the rabbit-hole; later mistakes her for his housemaid Mary Ann (TERM-0010) and serves as herald at the trial.

first_seen.quote: suddenly a White Rabbit with pink eyes ran close by her

terms.definition: A mouse Alice meets swimming in the Pool of Tears; leads the Caucus-race (TERM-0087) and begins to tell its sad "tale" (the shape-poem, TERM-0109) before storming off, offended by talk of cats and dogs.

terms.definition: A parrot among the birds soaked in the Pool of Tears; argues with Alice about age and later asks who Dinah is.

first_seen.quote: there were a Duck and a Dodo, a Lory and an Eaglet

terms.definition: One of the pool creatures; interrupts the Mouse's dry history recitation to ask what the archbishop "found."

first_seen.quote: there were a Duck and a Dodo, a Lory and an Eaglet

terms.definition: Proposes and organizes the Caucus-race (TERM-0087) to dry everyone off, then declares "everybody has won" and awards Alice a thimble as her own prize.

terms.definition: One of the pool creatures; tells the Dodo to "speak English" when its long words go unexplained.

first_seen.quote: there were a Duck and a Dodo, a Lory and an Eaglet

terms.definition: An old crab who moralizes to her young daughter about losing one's temper as the Mouse storms off from the Caucus-race gathering; the daughter snaps back at her.

first_seen.quote: an old Crab took the opportunity of saying to her daughter

terms.definition: One of the birds who hastily leaves after Alice praises Dinah's skill at catching birds, citing the night air.

terms.definition: A lizard sent down the chimney of the White Rabbit's house and kicked back out by giant Alice; reappears as a juror at the trial, where Alice steals his squeaking pencil and he is made to write with ink after his fingers.

terms.definition: Two guinea-pigs who tend the fallen Bill outside the White Rabbit's house; later cheer during the trial and are each suppressed by being tied head-first into a canvas bag.

terms.definition: A large blue caterpillar smoking a hookah (TERM-0079) atop a mushroom (TERM-0078); questions Alice's identity, tells her to "keep your temper," and reveals that the mushroom's two sides make her grow taller or shorter.

terms.definition: A mother bird who attacks Alice's elongated neck, convinced she is a serpent come to eat her eggs; unconvinced even when Alice claims to be a little girl.

first_seen.quote: a large pigeon had flown into her face

terms.definition: The Duchess's sneezing, star-fish-shaped infant, flung to Alice to nurse; turns into a pig in Alice's arms and trots off into the wood.

first_seen.quote: the Duchess was sitting on a three-legged stool in the middle, nursing a baby

terms.definition: A perpetually grinning cat, first seen in a tree near the Duchess's house, who can fade in and out of visibility (once leaving only the grin behind); directs Alice to the Hatter and March Hare, is nearly beheaded at the croquet ground, and vanishes before the executioner can act. Distinct from Dinah (TERM-0025), Alice's pet cat at home.

first_seen.quote: she was a little startled by seeing the Cheshire Cat sitting on a bough of a tree

terms.definition: Co-host with the Hatter of the never-ending tea party at his own house (chimneys shaped like ears, roof thatched with fur); described by the Cheshire Cat as mad, having gone mad the previous March.

first_seen.quote: in _that_ direction,” waving the other paw, “lives a March Hare

terms.definition: A perpetually sleepy mouse used as a cushion between the Hatter and March Hare at tea; tells the treacle-well story of Elsie, Lacie, and Tillie (TERM-0044) and reappears asleep at the trial.

first_seen.quote: a Dormouse was sitting between them, fast asleep

terms.definition: The Hatter's personification of time itself as a person ("him," not "it") whom he quarrelled with at a concert, freezing the tea party at six o'clock forever; a figure of speech, not a character who appears on stage.

terms.definition: A sleepy creature woken by the Queen to escort Alice to the Mock Turtle; explains that the Queen never actually executes anyone ("it's all her fancy") and joins the Mock Turtle in describing the Lobster Quadrille (TERM-0088).

first_seen.quote: They very soon came upon a Gryphon, lying fast asleep in the sun

terms.definition: A sobbing, sighing creature who was "a real Turtle" once; tells Alice of his undersea school under the Tortoise (TERM-0047) and sings "Turtle Soup" (TERM-0112). first_seen.quote: “It’s the thing Mock Turtle Soup is made from,” said the Queen

terms.definition: The Mock Turtle's old schoolmaster, an actual Turtle nicknamed "Tortoise" by his pupils because, as the Mock Turtle explains, "he taught us."

terms.definition: An old crab who taught "Laughing and Grief" (TERM-0102) at the undersea school; the Gryphon attended his lessons, the Mock Turtle did not.

terms.definition: An old conger-eel who came once a week to the undersea school to teach Drawling, Stretching, and Fainting in Coils (TERM-0098, TERM-0099, TERM-0100).

terms.definition: An enormous puppy Alice encounters in the wood after escaping the White Rabbit's house; she throws it a stick to distract it and escapes while it is not looking, before resuming her search for the mushroom.

terms.definition: A live flamingo Alice uses as a croquet mallet on the Queen's Croquet-Ground; keeps twisting its neck to look at her, ruining her swing.

first_seen.quote: the mallets live flamingoes

terms.definition: Live hedgehogs used as croquet balls on the Queen's Croquet-Ground; they unroll and crawl away mid-game, adding to the chaos.

first_seen.quote: the balls were live hedgehogs

terms.term: the ten soldiers, ten courtiers, and royal children
terms.original_name: the ten soldiers, ten courtiers, and royal children
terms.definition: The playing-card figures of the royal procession -- oblong club-shaped soldiers, diamond-covered courtiers, and heart-covered royal children -- who later double up as the croquet ground's arches. Part of the pack of cards (TERM-0090).

first_seen.quote: First came ten soldiers carrying clubs… next the ten courtiers

terms.definition: The overall dream-world Alice visits after following the White Rabbit down the rabbit-hole; the source text frames the entire adventure (chs. 1-11 and most of 12) as her dream, closed when her sister wakes her and reopened briefly in her sister's own closing reverie. Per user H1 ruling 5.2 A, Wonderland is dream-only space: every dream place is linked to a real waking-world detail it grows from (bible/geography.json grows_from pointers), and the waking world itself stays small and real (see TERM-0140 The Thames Valley Near Oxford). 'Wonderland (Alice's Dream)' is bible/geography.json's own name for its dream-layer root entry, not book wording.

first_seen.quote: half believed herself in Wonderland

terms.definition: The hole under the hedge that the White Rabbit pops down and Alice follows; it drops straight, then plunges into a long, slow fall past shelves and cupboards.

first_seen.quote: fortunately was just in time to see it pop down a large rabbit-hole under the hedge

terms.definition: A low hall lit by hanging lamps, lined with locked doors, holding the glass table with the golden key (TERM-0072); the little door behind a curtain leads to the beautiful garden (TERM-0062). It vanishes without explanation after Alice's swim in the Pool of Tears (ch004) and reappears in ch007.

first_seen.quote: she found herself in a long, low hall, which was lit up by a row of lamps

terms.definition: The salt-water pool formed by Alice's own tears when she was nine feet high; she and the animals she meets there swim to shore together.

first_seen.quote: she was in the pool of tears which she had wept when she was nine feet high

terms.definition: The thick wood Alice escapes into after fleeing the White Rabbit's house (meeting the puppy and the Caterpillar's mushroom clearing) and, later, the wood in front of which the March Hare's house stands.

first_seen.quote: she ran off as hard as she could, and soon found herself safe in a thick wood

terms.definition: A neat little house with a brass door-plate reading "W. RABBIT"; Alice grows too large inside it while fetching the Rabbit's gloves and fan, then escapes by shrinking after eating a pebble-turned-cake.

first_seen.quote: a bright brass plate with the name “W. RABBIT,” engraved upon it

terms.definition: A house about four feet high whose smoke-filled kitchen holds the pepper-soup, the sneezing baby, the cook, and the grinning cat on the hearth; entered by Alice via the Fish- and Frog-Footmen's door.

first_seen.quote: she came suddenly upon an open place, with a little house in it about four feet high

terms.definition: A large house with chimneys shaped like ears and a roof thatched with fur, where the endless tea party takes place under a tree out front.

first_seen.quote: the chimneys were shaped like ears and the roof was thatched with fur

terms.definition: The bright flower-bedded, fountain-cooled garden Alice glimpses through the little door off the long hall (TERM-0056) throughout the story; she finally reaches it at the end of ch007, and it opens into the Queen's Croquet-Ground.

terms.definition: A ridged and furrowed lawn beyond the garden where the Queen's court plays croquet with live flamingoes (TERM-0051) and hedgehogs (TERM-0052) and soldiers as arches; the rose-tree (TERM-0083) stands near its entrance.

first_seen.quote: Alice thought she had never seen such a curious croquet-ground in her life

terms.definition: The royal court of justice where the King (as judge, wig under crown) tries the Knave of Hearts for stealing the tarts, with a jury of twelve creatures, culminating in Alice's own testimony.

terms.definition: Real country Alice guesses she might fall through to the other side of the earth and arrive at, while falling down the rabbit-hole.

first_seen.quote: is this New Zealand or Australia?

first_seen.quote: London is the capital of Paris, and Paris is the capital of Rome

terms.definition: Real city named in the same jumbled Geography recitation, after which Alice concludes she must have turned into Mabel.

first_seen.quote: London is the capital of Paris, and Paris is the capital of Rome

terms.definition: Real country named in the Lobster Quadrille song (TERM-0111) as the far shore that makes the far-off dance worthwhile: "the nearer is to France."

terms.definition: A tiny golden key found on the glass table in the long hall (TERM-0056); it unlocks the little door to the beautiful garden but is repeatedly left out of Alice's reach by her own size changes.

first_seen.quote: there was nothing on it except a tiny golden key

terms.definition: A little bottle found on the glass table with a paper label reading "DRINK ME"; drinking it shrinks Alice to ten inches high.

first_seen.quote: with the words “DRINK ME,” beautifully printed on it in large letters

terms.definition: A small cake found under the glass table, with "EAT ME" marked in currants; eating it, Alice expects (wrongly, at first) to change size.

terms.definition: An empty jar labelled "ORANGE MARMALADE" that Alice takes from a shelf while falling down the rabbit-hole and tucks into a cupboard as she passes.

terms.term: the white kid gloves and fan
terms.original_name: the white kid gloves and fan

terms.original_name: the White Rabbit's trumpet and scroll
